title: Instruct the ignorant
tomorrow: how do you tell a king he's wrong and keep your head?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: walk with doubt. The stranger asked before he answered. Today, another road, and another man stuck on a page.

Two kinds of help. One coworker grabs your mouse, clicks four times, says see? and leaves you knowing nothing. Another pulls up a chair and asks where you got stuck. In the book of Acts, an official of the queen of Ethiopia sits in his chariot on a desert road, reading the prophet Isaiah, and he's stuck. A man named Philip runs up alongside and asks if he understands what he reads. The answer, in the Douay-Rheims: "And how can I, unless some man shew me?"
screen: `GRAB THE MOUSE, OR PULL UP A CHAIR?` → `A CHARIOT, A SCROLL, STUCK.` → `HOW CAN I, UNLESS SOME MAN SHEW ME?`

segments.voice: What he needed most wasn't a smarter book. It was someone beside him. And notice the old word in this work of mercy. Ignorant here doesn't mean foolish. It means not knowing. This man is no fool; Acts says he had charge of all the queen's treasure, and he's reading Isaiah on the road home. Now watch Philip. He runs to catch up; the learner doesn't have to come to him. He asks a question before he explains anything. He climbs up only when he's invited. And Acts says that, beginning at that very scripture, Philip told him about Jesus. He started on the page the man was already on. Soon the man sees water by the road and asks to be baptized. Then Philip is gone, and the man goes on his way rejoicing. The teacher doesn't stay at the center. Peter's first letter adds the tone: be ready to give a reason for your hope, "But with modesty and fear." Humbly, in other words. The Church lists instructing the ignorant among the spiritual works of mercy. In a parish, that's catechists teaching children, and adults who want to join the Church. But it's wider than a classroom: showing a new teammate the drill, teaching a kid a family recipe, explaining a prayer to a curious friend. Catch up, ask first, start on their page, then step back.
screen: `IGNORANT MEANS NOT KNOWING.` · `PHILIP RUNS TO CATCH UP.` · `HE STARTS ON THE MAN'S OWN PAGE.` · `WITH MODESTY AND FEAR.` · then, large: `SHARE WHAT YOU KNOW.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing you know how to do: a recipe, a move, a prayer, a shortcut. Out loud, explain its first step as if to someone beside you who has never seen it, slowly and in plain words. Then sit quietly with the person you'd most like to teach it to, and if you pray, you can pray for them.
Instruct the ignorant. Teach someone who doesn't know yet, starting where they are, and humbly.
Your line: share what you know. Philip ran to catch up, then let the learner lead. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1615 COUNTS.` → `THE WORKS OF MERCY · 9 OF 14.` → `TOMORROW: HOW DO YOU TELL A KING HE'S WRONG AND KEEP YOUR HEAD?`

howItsDone: Catholic parishes rely on volunteer catechists to teach children and to prepare adults who want to join the Church, and Catholics also take on this work informally at home and at work.
